Title: The Open Public Square: Why Social Media Platforms Must Be Legally Mandated to Host All Lawful Speech

The digital revolution has transformed communication, but it has also concentrated unprecedented power over public discourse in the hands of a few corporate platforms. As social media services and online platforms have evolved from niche forums into the indispensable infrastructure of modern civic life, they have simultaneously assumed the role of unaccountable arbiters of acceptable speech. This dual reality democratic self-governance. To preserve genuine free expression, prevent ideological gatekeeping, and recognize the functional reality of digital infrastructure, social media platforms and major online services must be legally required to host all content that complies with existing law, including lawful speech from hate groups. This obligation flows directly from two foundational principles: an absolute commitment to free speech within legal boundaries, and the application of common carrier doctrine to essential digital conduits.

The philosophical and constitutional bedrock of liberal democracy rests on the premise that free expression must be protected not when it is agreeable, but precisely when it is offensive. The classic free speech tradition, from John Stuart Mill’s harm principle to Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr.’s marketplace of ideas, holds that truth emerges through open contestation, not preemptive suppression. When platforms are permitted to remove lawful speech based on subjective judgments of offensiveness, ideological alignment, or perceived social harm, they do not protect society; they privatize censorship. Absolute free speech, properly understood, does not tolerate incitement to imminent violence, true threats, fraud, child exploitation, or defamation. But it does tolerate deeply repugnant viewpoints, historical revisionism, religious intolerance, and extremist political organizing, provided such speech remains within the legal boundary. The moment we allow private entities to draw lines beyond what the law prohibits, we cede democratic discourse to corporate risk-aversion and political pressure. The remedy to vile but lawful speech is not silence, but counter-speech, transparency, and citizen resilience.

This free speech imperative is reinforced by the functional reality of modern platforms: they operate as common carriers. Historically, common carrier obligations were applied to railroads, telegraph lines, telephone networks, and postal services precisely because they provided essential conduits for public communication and commerce. The core principle was simple and democratically vital: entities that offer general transmission services to the public cannot discriminate against lawful messages based on their content, sender, or viewpoint. They must remain neutral conduits, carrying all lawful traffic without editorial interference. Today’s social media platforms and major online hosting services perform the exact same function at planetary scale. They provide the architecture through which citizens organize, journalists report, businesses operate, and movements mobilize. When these platforms selectively deplatform, shadowban, or algorithmically suppress lawful content, they violate the neutral carriage principle that has long governed essential communications infrastructure. Legally classifying dominant platforms as common carriers would not strip them of innovation or user interface design; it would simply require them to honor the foundational promise of open, nondiscriminatory transmission for lawful speech.

Critics routinely raise three objections to this framework: that platforms are not utilities, that hosting hate speech causes real harm, and that forced hosting violates platform autonomy. Each objection collapses under scrutiny. First, platform utility is not a binary category but a functional reality. When a handful of services command billions of users, serve as primary news distributors, host political campaigning, and function as de facto public squares, their scale and indispensability justify common carrier obligations. Second, while hate speech can inflict psychological and social harm, democratic societies have long accepted that the greater danger lies in allowing authorities private or public to dictate what may be said. Empowering platforms to preemptively silence lawful viewpoints creates a chilling effect that disproportionately impacts marginalized dissidents, minority religions, and unpopular political movements just as much as it fails to eliminate bigotry. Third, platform autonomy is not absolute when it intersects with essential public infrastructure. Telephone companies did not lose their business model when required to carry all lawful calls; email providers do not claim editorial rights over message content. Requiring platforms to host lawful speech does not force them to algorithmically amplify, monetize, or recommend it. It simply requires them to maintain a neutral, accessible repository for lawful user-generated content, while preserving robust, legally grounded exceptions for genuinely unlawful material.

Implementing this vision requires careful statutory design. Legislation should establish clear scale and market dominance thresholds to trigger common carrier classification, avoiding burdens on small startups or niche communities. Platforms would be mandated to host all content that does not violate existing criminal or civil law, with transparent, appealable processes for reviewing alleged illegal material. Independent oversight bodies, operating at arm’s length from political influence, could audit compliance without evaluating content merit. Crucially, users must retain robust opt-out, filtering, and blocking tools, ensuring that while speech remains hosted, individuals control what enters their personal feeds. This framework respects both the right to speak and the right not to listen, while preventing corporate entities from unilaterally erasing lawful expression from the digital record.

A society that outsources its discourse to unaccountable moderation teams invites ideological fragmentation, democratic disenfranchisement, and the normalization of digital censorship. The alternative is not chaos, but principle: anchor platform obligations in absolute free speech boundaries and common carrier neutrality. Legal mandates to host all lawful content, including the speech of hate groups, do not endorse bigotry; they defend the structural conditions under which bigotry can be openly identified, debated, and rejected. By treating dominant digital platforms as the modern equivalents of public communication infrastructure, we restore transparency, accountability, and democratic equality to the online public square. The cost of free speech is the discomfort of encountering ideas we despise. The cost of abandoning it is the quiet, incremental surrender of who may speak at all.

A legal hosting mandate is framed as a structural barrier against such coordination by requiring platforms to remain neutral regardless of political pressure.

Encouragement of Alternative Moderation & User Agency Under a host-all-legal model, proponents often suggest shifting responsibility to users through enhanced filtering tools, third-party moderation layers, or interoperable networks. This preserves speech while allowing individuals to curate their own feeds according to personal or community standards.

This position exists within a broader, highly contested debate. Critics raise concerns about real-world harms, the rights of private companies to set terms of service, the practical and safety challenges of operating at scale, and the tension between unrestricted speech and other fundamental rights. Legal and regulatory approaches vary significantly across jurisdictions, with many governments pursuing transparency mandates, due process requirements, or risk-based frameworks rather than absolute hosting requirements.

Summary

Advocates of legally mandating platforms to host all legal content ground their arguments in free speech absolutism, distrust of unaccountable private censorship, and the belief that open digital forums best serve democratic discourse, intellectual progress, and historical safeguards for dissenting voices. The stance remains a central reference point in ongoing discussions about platform governance, speech rights, and the balance between expression, safety, and private autonomy online.

In the annals of liberal democracy, the principle of free speech has always been a radical and often uncomfortable commitment. It is not a principle designed to protect popular speech, which needs no defense, but to shield the controversial, the dissenting, and the despised from the tyranny of the majority and the power of the state. In the 21st century, the public square has migrated from the physical commons to digital platforms, creating an unprecedented constitutional crisis. A handful of private corporations now act as the arbiters of public discourse, wielding the power to silence voices with the flick of an algorithm. To preserve the foundational tenets of a free society, we must legally bind social media platforms and online services to a common carrier obligation, requiring them to host all legal content, without exception. This includes the speech of hate groups, not because we endorse it, but because the alternative—the sanction of corporate censorship—is a far greater threat to liberty.

The bedrock of this argument rests upon the absolute free speech principle best articulated by John Stuart Mill: the "marketplace of ideas." Mill argued that truth can only emerge from the free and robust competition of all viewpoints, even those we find false or dangerous. When we suppress an idea, we lose the opportunity to refute it, to strengthen our own convictions through debate, and to risk the possibility that the silenced idea contains a kernel of truth we have yet to consider. Social media platforms, by their very design, are the ultimate marketplace of ideas. They are the primary venue for political organization, journalistic reporting, and community building. When these platforms engage in content moderation beyond what is strictly illegal, they are no longer neutral marketplaces but curated galleries. They pick winners and losers in the battle of ideas, a power that no unelected corporate board should ever possess. To grant them the authority to ban "hate speech" is to grant them the authority to define it, a line that is notoriously subjective and prone to shift with political winds. The speech of one generation’s radical is often the next generation’s accepted truth; allowing corporations to police this process is to cede the future of our discourse to their marketing departments and liability concerns.

Opponents of this view often conflate the protection of hateful ideas with the incitement of violence. This is a deliberate and dangerous conflation. The law already rightly distinguishes between speech and action. Incitement to imminent lawless action is a crime and should be prosecuted as such, both online and off. However, speech that is merely offensive, bigoted, or hateful, while morally abhorrent, remains legal. The proposal to mandate content hosting is squarely in the realm of legal speech. The argument is not that platforms should host threats of violence or criminal conspiracy, but that they should not be the judges of political opinion, no matter how vile. The solution to bad speech, as the classic liberal adage goes, is more speech. Sunlight is the most powerful disinfectant. Forcing hate speech from the public view does not eliminate it; it drives it into encrypted echo chambers where it can fester, be normalized, and radicalize its adherents without challenge. In the open, it can be met with counter-protest, ridicule, and reasoned refutation, allowing society to see its bankruptcy for itself.

This is where the legal doctrine of common carrier status becomes essential. Historically, a common carrier is a private entity that offers its services to the general public without discrimination, such as telephone companies, railroads, and utility providers. We do not allow the telephone company to terminate your service because they disapprove of your political conversations, nor can the electric company shut off your power due to your unpopular associations. We impose these obligations because these services have become essential infrastructure for modern life. Social media platforms have clearly crossed this threshold. They are no longer optional diversions; they are integral to employment, commerce, news consumption, and political participation. To function in society without a presence on major platforms is to be functionally silenced. Reclassifying them as common carriers would strip them of their editorial discretion and compel them to act as neutral conduits for information, upholding their obligation to serve all users equally, regardless of the content of their message, so long as that content is legal.

In conclusion, the choice is not between a civil society and a chaotic one. It is a choice between a society governed by the principles of free expression and one governed by the terms of service of a handful of tech monopolies. The path of censorship is a seductively easy one, promising a sanitized world free from offense. But it is a path that leads to a sterile, controlled, and ultimately unfree discourse, where the only permissible ideas are those approved by corporate gatekeepers. The harder path—the path of true liberty—requires us to defend the rights of those whose speech we find most repugnant. By legally obligating social media platforms to act as common carriers and host all legal content, we affirm our commitment to the marketplace of ideas, reject the dangerous concentration of corporate power, and ensure that the digital public square remains a vibrant, if often messy, forum for the unfettered exchange of ideas that is the lifeblood of a free democracy.

Core Principles Underpinning the Argument

This position is built on two foundational ideas:

  1. Unrestricted Free Speech as a Paramount Good: The belief that the free exchange of ideas, without exception, is essential for a functioning democracy, the pursuit of truth, and individual liberty.
  2. Distrust of Private Corporate Power: The concern that a small number of unelected tech executives should not have the authority to act as censors, shaping public discourse according to their own values or commercial interests.

Based on these principles, proponents make the following arguments:

Proponents argue that social media platforms are no longer just private businesses; they are the modern equivalent of the public square.

The government cannot censor speech based on viewpoint, and neither should these essential digital spaces. To allow them to do so is to effectively privatize the public square and subject fundamental rights to corporate terms of service.

2. The "Marketplace of Ideas" Argument

This is a classic concept, most famously articulated by John Stuart Mill. The belief is that the truth will emerge from the competition of ideas in a free and open environment.

  • Sunlight is the Best Disinfectant: Forcing hateful ideas into the open allows them to be seen, challenged, and refuted with better ideas. Censorship, by contrast, drives these ideas underground where they can fester, become more extreme, and spread without opposition.
  • Counter-Speech is More Effective: The most powerful response to bad speech is not silence, but more speech. When a hate group posts something, other users are free to condemn it, debunk its claims, and present a superior, more inclusive message. This robust debate is seen as healthier and more effective in the long run than simple deletion.
  • Avoiding the "Streisand Effect": Censorship can inadvertently give hateful or fringe ideas more attention and credibility. When a group is de-platformed, it can create "martyrs" and lend them an aura of forbidden truth, making their message more appealing to some. Allowing them to speak freely robs them of this perceived persecution.

3. The "Preventing Corporate Censorship" Argument

This argument focuses on the danger of allowing private companies to become the arbiters of acceptable speech.

  • Unelected and Unaccountable Power: Tech CEOs and content moderation teams are not elected and are not accountable to the public. Their decisions to remove content can be based on personal bias, political pressure, or the desire to attract advertisers, not on principled grounds.
  • Censorship by Proxy: This concept suggests that even if the government is legally barred from censoring speech, it can achieve the same result by pressuring private platforms to do its bidding. A law mandating neutrality prevents this "censorship by proxy."
  • The Chilling Effect: When platforms have vague and ever-changing rules, users will self-censor. They may avoid expressing controversial, dissenting, or merely unpopular opinions for fear of being suspended or banned. This "chilling effect" impoverishes public discourse and makes it more bland and conformist.

4. The "Slippery Slope" Argument

Proponents argue that any censorship power will inevitably be abused and expanded over time.

  • Who Defines "Hate"? The definition of "hate speech" is subjective and fluid. What one person considers hateful, another may see as legitimate political or religious expression.
  • The Inevitable Expansion of Bans: The argument is that once a platform starts by banning universally condemned groups like neo-Nazis, the definition of "hate" will slowly expand to include less extreme groups, then mainstream political opposition, and eventually anyone who challenges the prevailing consensus of the platform's leadership. The goal is to draw a firm, bright-line rule: only illegal content (like direct incitement to violence) can be banned.

5. The "Principled Consistency" Argument

This is a more philosophical argument about the nature of rights.

  • Rights are Not Conditional: The principle of free speech is only meaningful if it applies to the speech one finds most repugnant. Defending the right to speak for popular or agreeable groups requires no courage. The true test of a commitment to free speech is defending the rights of those whose views you despise.
  • Let the Law Decide: The legal system already provides a framework for limiting speech that causes direct, tangible harm (e.g., defamation, incitement to imminent lawless action, true threats). This argument posits that this legal line is the only one that should be drawn. It is not the place of a private company to create its own, more restrictive legal code for speech.

Summary of the Viewpoint

In essence, the argument for legally mandating platforms to host all legal content is a trade-off. It prioritizes:

  • Maximum Freedom of Expression: Above all else.
  • Individual Agency: Trusting users to navigate information and counter bad ideas on their own.
  • Distrust of Centralized Authority: Whether governmental or corporate.

It accepts that the cost of these principles is a more toxic and unpleasant online environment, filled with ideas that many find abhorrent. However, proponents believe this cost is outweighed by the long-term benefits of preventing censorship, ensuring a robust marketplace of ideas, and protecting fundamental liberty from the power of unaccountable private corporations.

If we take seriously the idea of absolute free speech and treat these platforms as essential conduits for expression, then there is a powerful case to be made that they should be legally required to host all legal content. This argument rests on two sturdy pillars: the principle of absolute free speech, and the analogy to common-carrier or public-utility infrastructure.   1. Absolute free speech and the moral logic of exposure The first line of argument is philosophical and constitutional: speech should be free, and the state’s power to regulate speech should be minimized. If speech is a fundamental medium through which individuals exercise autonomy, participate in civic life, and persuade others, then silencing voices—whether popular or unpopular—undermines the very purpose of a free society. When platforms decide that certain viewpoints or groups will not be permitted to speak, they perform a de facto veto that resembles a government censorship, even though the platform is a private actor. The logic of free speech isn’t merely about protecting the loud or the powerful; it is about ensuring a spectrum broad enough for ideas to collide, be challenged, and be tested in the public arena.

Proponents of absolute free speech argue that the best antidote to bad ideas is not censorship but more speech: exposure, argument, and counter-speech. The marketplace of ideas only works if speakers have access to a broad audience, and if audiences can encounter, critique, and reject arguments they dislike. Requiring platforms to host all lawful content preserves the integrity of that marketplace by preventing private gatekeeping that privileges certain ideologies, perspectives, or brands over others. It treats social media as a neutral conduit rather than a value-laden editor, and it grounds policy in the principle that access to the platform is a public good that should not be curtailed on the basis of viewpoint.

  1. Common carriage and the infrastructure analogy A second pillar is the common-carrier or public-utility analogy. Telecommunication networks, the postal service, and similar infrastructures are treated as essential services that must carry messages from everyone to everyone else, without privileging some speakers over others. The reason is simple: society depends on reliable, non-discriminatory channels of communication. If one person cannot send a message because the channel arbitrarily blocks it, the channel ceases to be a neutral conduit and becomes a gatekeeper.

Applied to the digital realm, social media platforms perform the function of a vast, instantaneous communications infrastructure. They enable individuals to broadcast ideas to large audiences, mobilize communities, and challenge prevailing narratives. If platforms were empowered to selectively deny transmission based on the content or the speaker’s identity—for example, silencing groups that are legally permissible but deemed “undesirable”—they would resemble editors who decide what counts as legitimate input for the public square. The common-carrier model argues for a legally mandated neutrality: platforms should facilitate transmission of all lawful messages unless there is a compelling, legally recognized reason to restrict a specific piece of content (e.g., illegal activity or direct threats). The normative payoff is straightforward: the public gains the broadest possible access to voices and information, and power to censor rests in duly enacted law rather than corporate policy.

  1. Neutrality, equality, and the risk of viewpoint discrimination A related argument concerns neutrality and equality before the platform. If platforms curate content, even with the best intentions, they inevitably privilege certain viewpoints over others. Algorithms, human moderators, and policy funnels are imperfect systems that reflect human biases, organizational incentives, and political pressures. An absolute hosting obligation reduces the problem of bias by removing platform editors from the role of de facto arbiters of who may speak and who may be heard. In a regime that treats platforms as common carriers, the default position is inclusive: lawful content should be transmitted, and any exclusions must be narrowly and transparently justified by law, not by corporate preference or market position.

This does not imply that platforms lose the capacity to enforce safety or criminal-law boundaries. The argument recognizes that content that is illegal or directly dangerous remains subject to legal prohibitions. But it insists that the line between lawful and unlawful content must be drawn by law, not by private policy, and that the mere risk of harm is not a sufficient ground for blanket exclusion of lawful speech. In effect, a robust hosting obligation grounds moderation in narrowly tailored, legally defined exceptions rather than broad editorial discretion that can be weaponized to suppress dissent or minority voices.

  1. Safety, harm mitigation, and the practical design of hosting obligations A common concern is that hosting all lawful content would magnify harm, harassment, incitement, and extremist propaganda. The strongest answer on that point is to separate the function of hosting from the function of enforcing safety and legality. Platforms can, and should, maintain mechanisms to remove illegal content or block wrongdoing (e.g., child exploitation material, threats of violence, doxxing) without engaging in broad suppression of lawful speech. Hosting obligations would be paired with strong, transparent, and law-aligned safety rules that permit removal of illegal content and actionable threats, while preserving the broadest possible space for lawful, even if controversial or hateful, speech.

To make this workable, several design and governance features would be essential:

  • Content neutrality: hosting rules should be applied in a content-neutral way, not guided by political or ideological preferences.
  • Transparency and accountability: platforms disclose how content is transmitted, how moderation decisions are made, and how exemptions are applied.
  • Due process and appeal: users should have a clear process to challenge removals or restrictions, with independent review.

A practical legislative approach would define:

  • The scope of “legal content” as content that is not illegal under criminal or civil law and not subject to an active court order prohibiting dissemination.
  • The degree of hosting obligation, with explicit exemptions for illegal content, incitement to imminent violence, child exploitation, and other messages proscribed by law.
  • Oversight and enforcement mechanisms, including independent regulator(s), periodic sunset reviews, and penalties for non-compliance.
  • A transition framework that protects platform viability, preserves innovation, and avoids abrupt destabilization of online services.

Conclusion: a principled case for a digital common carrier If we accept the premise that social media platforms are essential communications infrastructure, and if we accept the philosophical and democratic value of maximal exposure to competing ideas, then a policy shift toward a legal obligation to host all lawful content follows logically. Should major online platforms be legally required to host all lawful content? The common-carrier and absolute free-speech case—plus its limits

The modern public sphere runs through privately owned platforms: social networks, video hosts, app stores, payment processors, and cloud services. Because these companies mediate who can speak and who can be heard, some scholars and policymakers argue that certain large, structurally essential online services should be treated more like common carriers—telephone networks, postal services, or railroads—than like publishers. On this view, platforms should be legally required to carry all lawful content, even if it is offensive or socially harmful, because the alternative grants private firms power over political speech that resembles censorship by proxy. The common-carrier framework, paired with an “absolute” conception of free speech, aims to make access to essential communications infrastructure depend on law, not corporate discretion.

1) The absolute free-speech premise: legality as the only workable boundary

A core claim behind “must-carry for lawful content” is that speech regulation becomes arbitrary once it moves beyond legality. The law already draws lines: true threats, defamation, unlawful harassment, certain forms of incitement, and other categories may be restricted. Everything else is, by definition, legal expression. If platforms may remove lawful speech based on internal policies or shifting cultural norms, then the boundary of public participation is set by private power rather than democratic process.

Proponents argue that legality is the only stable, objective, and reviewable standard. Corporate content rules often rely on contested definitions (“hate,” “misinformation,” “extremism,” “harm”), which can be inconsistently enforced. The result is unpredictable suppression that can fall disproportionately on unpopular viewpoints, dissidents, minority religious movements, or politically inconvenient journalism. In an “absolute free speech” model, the answer to harmful ideas is counter-speech, social condemnation, and lawful prosecution of actual crimes—not discretionary removal of speech that has not crossed a legal line.

2) Platforms as private governors: the democratic legitimacy problem

Another argument is institutional: major platforms operate as quasi-governments. They set rules; they adjudicate disputes; they impose penalties up to effective “exile” from core channels of communication; and they do so with limited transparency and weak procedural protections. When a handful of companies can effectively deplatform a movement, an individual, or a controversial cause, the capacity for democratic deliberation may be narrowed by managerial preferences, advertiser pressure, or political lobbying.

A legal must-carry obligation is presented as a way to restore legitimacy. In this framing, the state is not compelling endorsement of speech; it is preventing private gatekeepers from controlling a critical layer of civic infrastructure. The principle resembles anti-discrimination or access requirements applied to essential services: if a service is sufficiently central to participation in society, denial of access should require a strong, public justification.

3) The common-carrier analogy: nondiscrimination for essential conduits

The common-carrier model historically applies where (a) the service is a conduit rather than a speaker, (b) market power or network effects make exit difficult, and (c) nondiscrimination is necessary to prevent private chokepoints. Telephone networks carry conversations without judging them; postal services deliver messages without reading them; freight rail carries goods without picking ideological favorites. Advocates say that major social platforms and online infrastructure increasingly satisfy the same conditions:

  • Network effects and lock-in: leaving the largest platform can mean losing an audience, economic opportunity, and social ties.
  • Bottleneck control: app stores, payment rails, and hosting services can cut off entire organizations, even when the underlying content is lawful.
  • Practical indispensability: for many people, these services are the primary means of participating in civic and cultural life.

From this perspective, a must-carry rule is not about declaring platforms “the public square” in a metaphorical sense, but about recognizing functional reality: when a private entity becomes a choke point for communication, neutrality duties can be justified to protect pluralism.

4) Benefits claimed by must-carry advocates

Supporters of mandatory hosting for lawful speech claim several concrete benefits:

  1. Viewpoint neutrality: the most direct protection against ideological suppression.
  2. Predictability: legality is clearer than internal trust-and-safety standards that shift with politics or public pressure.
  3. Reduced politicization of moderation: platforms could focus on spam, fraud, and technical integrity while leaving contested political judgments to democratic institutions and courts.
  4. Competitive fairness: smaller speakers and unpopular groups would not be at the mercy of reputationally motivated enforcement.
  5. Free-speech culture: tolerating offensive speech, while countering it, is seen as strengthening societal resilience and protecting dissent.

This logic extends, controversially, to all lawful speech including speech associated with hate groups: if it is truly legal, the argument goes, then forcing private intermediaries to carry it prevents “speech blacklists” that could later be used against any minority viewpoint. The remedy for bigotry is condemnation and counter-organizing—not empowering gatekeepers to decide what beliefs may be aired.

5) The strongest objections: why the analogy is contested

Even if the common-carrier and absolute free-speech logic is internally coherent, major objections challenge whether it should be adopted as law.

A. Platforms are not mere conduits.
Many services algorithmically curate, recommend, and amplify content. Critics argue that this makes them closer to editors than to phone companies. Requiring them to “carry” and potentially recommend all lawful content can look like compelled speech or compelled association, raising constitutional and moral concerns.

B. “Legal” does not mean “non-harmful.”
A great deal of harmful conduct can be legal: targeted harassment that evades statutory definitions, doxxing in jurisdictions without strong protections, extremist recruitment rhetoric crafted to avoid incitement standards, and disinformation that is not defamatory. Opponents argue that forcing hosting of such material imposes real-world costs—especially on vulnerable communities—while providing speakers a subsidized megaphone.

C. Safety and usability depend on moderation.
Even advocates of broad expression often accept the need to combat spam, scams, and coordinated manipulation. The line between “content moderation” and “service integrity” is blurry. A rigid must-carry rule could reduce a platform’s ability to maintain a usable environment, driving users away and undermining the very speech ecosystem the rule aims to protect.

D. Property, autonomy, and pluralism concerns.
Requiring private entities to host speech they find abhorrent can be framed as an intrusion on autonomy. There is also a pluralism argument: a world with many communities setting their own norms can be valuable. A single legal mandate of maximal permissiveness may flatten the diversity of online spaces and reduce the ability to build moderated communities (e.g., support groups, youth spaces, professional forums).

E. Implementation and jurisdictional conflict.
Legality differs across countries. A global platform faces conflicting obligations (e.g., hate-speech laws in some jurisdictions and stronger speech protections in others). A must-carry requirement in one country could collide with takedown obligations in another, forcing geofencing, fragmentation, or overbroad compliance.

6) A narrower version: “common carriage for dominance,” plus due process

Because of these objections, some propose narrower reforms rather than an absolute must-carry rule: apply nondiscrimination and carriage duties only to truly dominant, infrastructure-like services; require transparent rules, notice, appeals, and consistent enforcement; and preserve the ability to remove content that is lawful but functionally abusive (e.g., coordinated harassment, spam, impersonation). This approach aims to protect speech without turning every platform into an unmoderated space.

Conclusion

The absolute free-speech/common-carrier case rests on a powerful concern: when private platforms become the gatekeepers of public communication, discretionary moderation can resemble censorship without democratic accountability. A legality-only standard and must-carry duty promises neutrality, predictability, and protection for unpopular speakers. Yet the strongest counterarguments note that platforms are not passive conduits, that legal speech can still impose severe harms, and that compelled hosting can undermine safety, community autonomy, and practical governance. Whether society should adopt a must-carry regime thus turns on a difficult judgment: how to prevent private chokepoints from controlling civic discourse while preserving the capacity to limit harassment, manipulation, and the real-world harms that can flourish even within the boundaries of formal legality.

The Case for Requiring Online Platforms to Host All Legal Speech

In a free society, the right to speak means little if private institutions can decide which lawful ideas may reach the public. Today, a small number of social-media companies and online services exercise extraordinary control over political debate, cultural expression, journalism, and public organizing. They can remove users, suppress posts, demonetize publications, and restrict access to audiences with little transparency and often no meaningful appeal. This concentration of communicative power threatens the basic premise of free expression. Social-media platforms and major online services should therefore be legally required to host all content that is lawful—including speech produced by hate groups—subject only to narrowly defined exceptions such as criminal threats, incitement, fraud, and unlawful harassment.

The central principle is simple: speech should be judged by law, not by the private preferences of corporations. Hate speech is repugnant, but repugnance is not a sufficient reason for censorship. A legal system committed to freedom must distinguish between expression that is offensive and expression that causes legally recognized harm. If a group advocates racial supremacy, religious hatred, or ethnic exclusion without making a true threat or directly urging imminent violence, its ideas should be answered with criticism, organizing, education, and counter-speech—not suppression.

This position does not defend hate groups morally. It defends the broader social principle that governments and dominant communications platforms should not be empowered to decide which political or ideological views are too hateful to be heard. Once that power exists, it rarely remains confined to the most universally condemned speakers. Definitions of “hate speech” vary across cultures, institutions, and political movements. A rule created to silence neo-Nazis could later be applied to activists, religious minorities, dissidents, or unpopular critics of government policy. Absolute free-speech principles are valuable precisely because they prevent authorities from deciding that certain ideas are beyond public discussion.

The danger is particularly acute online because platforms have become essential forums for public life. Social networks are not merely private clubs or personal blogs. They function as news distributors, campaign venues, marketplaces, publishing systems, and meeting places for civic movements. A person excluded from a major platform may lose access to customers, colleagues, journalists, political audiences, and communities. When a handful of companies control these channels, their content-moderation decisions can have consequences comparable to traditional censorship, even if the censor is technically a private corporation.

This is where common-carrier principles become relevant. Historically, common carriers—such as telephone companies, railroads, and telecommunications providers—have been subject to duties of nondiscrimination because they provide essential services while operating network infrastructure that the public relies upon. A telephone company generally cannot refuse to connect a customer because it dislikes the customer’s political views. The point is not that every business must host every message, but that entities occupying a uniquely powerful communications role should not arbitrarily discriminate among lawful users.

Large online platforms increasingly resemble common carriers in practical function. They benefit from network effects that make alternatives difficult to use. A competing website may exist, but it cannot easily replicate the audience, infrastructure, search visibility, social connections, and economic opportunities concentrated on the dominant platform. In such circumstances, “just use another service” is often not a meaningful answer. Legal obligations should reflect the platform’s public importance rather than its preferred corporate label.

A hosting requirement would also improve democratic accountability. If platforms must carry all lawful viewpoints, they could no longer quietly determine which movements receive visibility and which are effectively erased. Political disputes would remain disputes among citizens instead of becoming opaque decisions by corporate policy teams. Users could encounter hateful arguments and respond publicly, exposing their weaknesses. Journalists could document extremist movements rather than relying on leaks or fragmented archives. Researchers could study radicalization more accurately. Sunlight and rebuttal are often more effective than forcing dangerous ideas into hidden corners of the internet.

Opponents argue that mandatory hosting would violate the platforms’ own freedom of speech. Private companies, they contend, have a First Amendment right to decide what appears in their publications. That argument has force for genuinely editorial enterprises, such as newspapers that select and arrange articles as part of a distinct expressive product. But it is less persuasive when applied to massive platforms that primarily provide neutral infrastructure for user-generated communication. A social-media post is ordinarily understood as the user’s speech, not the platform’s endorsement. Requiring a telephone network to carry a call does not mean the network supports what the caller says; similarly, requiring a platform to host lawful content need not attribute that content to the platform.

A carefully designed law could preserve the distinction between hosting and endorsement. Platforms could place labels on posts, provide context, limit algorithmic promotion, allow users to block or filter material, and clearly state that user content does not represent the company. They could also remove content that is illegal: true threats, targeted incitement to imminent violence, child sexual abuse material, unlawful fraud, and other categories already recognized by law. Critics also warn that hate speech can cause real harm, especially to vulnerable communities. That concern must be taken seriously. But a broad censorship power may itself create serious harms by allowing dominant institutions to define acceptable opinion and suppress marginalized or dissident voices. Users are capable of blocking, muting, or ignoring content they find offensive without requiring the platform to annihilate it. In conclusion, the survival of free discourse in the digital age depends on treating social media as a common carrier. We must legally bind these platforms to the principle of neutrality, ensuring that no legal voice—no matter how reviled or repulsive—is erased from the public square. Telegraph and telephone companies could not refuse service based on the content of messages or the identity of speakers. This principle extended beyond transportation and communication to include any business "affected with a public interest," recognizing that certain private enterprises perform functions so essential to public welfare that they must accommodate all lawful users.

Social media platforms fit squarely within this tradition. They explicitly market themselves as open platforms for communication, invite billions of users to create and share content, and derive their value from the network effects generated by this openness. The First Amendment's protection extends to all legal speech, not merely speech that majorities find palatable or that aligns with contemporary moral sensibilities. This principle has protected speech ranging from communist advocacy during the Cold War to neo-Nazi marches through Jewish neighborhoods. The Supreme Court has consistently held that the proper response to offensive speech is more speech, not censorship, recognizing that empowering authorities to suppress disfavored viewpoints poses greater dangers than the speech itself.

The Case for Mandatory Content Hosting: Platforms as Digital Common Carriers

Introduction

As social media platforms have become the primary venues for public discourse, a critical legal and philosophical question has emerged: should these platforms be required to host all legal content, regardless of how objectionable it might be? This essay argues they should, on the grounds of free speech principles and common carrier doctrine—while acknowledging this is a genuinely contested question with serious counterarguments worth taking seriously.

The Common Carrier Argument

Common carrier law traditionally applied to telephone companies, railroads, and utilities—entities that, because they control essential infrastructure with no reasonable substitutes, are barred from discriminating among customers. The logic holds that when a service becomes essential infrastructure for participation in public life, the provider forfeits ordinary discretion over who may use it.

Proponents argue major platforms now meet this threshold. Facebook, YouTube, and X aren't niche services—they're the modern public square, essential for political organizing, commerce, and civic participation. When a handful of companies control the infrastructure of public discourse, their content decisions function less like a bookstore's curation and more like a utility company deciding whose calls to connect.

The Free Speech Rationale

The argument extends beyond infrastructure to values. Advocates contend that:

  • Viewpoint neutrality prevents concentration of power. If platforms can suppress "legal but awful" speech at will, a small number of executives gain outsized power to shape public discourse—arguably more dangerous than government censorship because it's less accountable and less visible.

  • The marketplace of ideas requires access, not just permission. Legal speech that cannot find an audience is functionally suppressed. If mainstream platforms exclude a viewpoint, that viewpoint effectively disappears from public life, even though it was never outlawed.

  • Slippery slope concerns are legitimate. Definitions of "hate speech" or "misinformation" have proven historically elastic and politically contested. Handing platforms discretion to police these categories invites inconsistent, ideologically skewed enforcement—a pattern critics say is already visible.

Why This Argument Struggles

Having laid out the strongest version of this case, it's worth being direct: this argument faces serious problems that make it, in my assessment, ultimately unpersuasive.

Platforms are not phone lines. Common carrier obligations applied to conduits that don't organize, algorithmically rank, or amplify content. Social media platforms curate by design—recommendation algorithms, trending sections, and feeds all involve editorial choices. Forcing "neutral" hosting doesn't eliminate this; it just forces platforms to make those choices under a legal fiction of neutrality.

Compelled hosting is itself a speech issue. The First Amendment (in the U.S. context) protects private entities from being forced to carry speech, not just from government suppression of speech. Requiring a platform to host content it finds abhorrent is a different but equally real infringement on associational and editorial freedom—one the Supreme Court affirmed in Moody v. NetChoice (2024) by recognizing platforms' own expressive interests in content moderation.

Hate speech carries real-world costs platforms don't have to underwrite. Harassment campaigns, coordinated disinformation, and violent extremist recruitment have documented links to platform amplification (e.g., Myanmar, January 6th). Legal categories of speech and harmless speech are not identical—defamation, targeted harassment, and incitement often occupy legal gray zones that platforms are better positioned to manage contextually than a blunt "must-host" mandate would allow.

Multiplicity undercuts the monopoly premise. Unlike historical utilities, there are competing platforms, decentralized alternatives (Mastodon, Bluesky), and the open web itself. No single company controls the only wire into your house.

Conclusion

The common carrier and free speech framing for mandatory content hosting raises a genuine and important concern: unaccountable concentrated power over discourse deserves scrutiny. But the proposed remedy—stripping platforms of editorial discretion entirely—misdiagnoses the problem. It treats curation as inherently illegitimate rather than recognizing that some editorial judgment is unavoidable once you have algorithms and design choices at all. The better path likely lies in transparency requirements, interoperability mandates, and antitrust enforcement that preserve competition and disclosure without compelling platforms to become indiscriminate hosts of any legal speech, however vile. The problem is concentrated power; the solution is diffusing that power, not eliminating judgment altogether.

The Case for Mandatory Hosting: Social Media as Common Carriers of All Legal Speech

Social media platforms and major online services have become the de facto public squares of the twenty-first century. They are not quaint private clubs or small-town newspapers; they are essential infrastructure for political discourse, commerce, journalism, and cultural exchange. Free Speech Is Not a Popularity Contest

The classical liberal understanding of free speech, crystallized in the American First Amendment and echoed in the broader Western tradition, is not a limited privilege granted only to polite or popular opinions. It is a negative restraint on power: the state may not use its coercive monopoly on violence to punish or suppress expression that falls short of narrow, well-defined exceptions (incitement to imminent violence, true threats, fraud, defamation, and obscenity as historically understood). Speech that is merely offensive, hateful, racist, sexist, or ideologically extreme remains legal in the United States and in most liberal democracies when it does not cross those lines.

The same principle applies with even greater force to private platforms that have achieved near-monopoly status over public discourse. When Facebook, YouTube, Twitter (pre-Musk), TikTok, or Google collectively control the distribution of information to billions, their decision to remove lawful content is functionally equivalent to censorship on a societal scale. The marketplace of ideas cannot function if gatekeepers are permitted to exclude entire categories of thought they dislike. John Stuart Mill’s harm principle is instructive here: the only justification for limiting speech is demonstrable harm, not emotional discomfort or ideological disagreement. Hate groups expressing legal viewpoints—no matter how repulsive—do not lose their rights simply because major corporations find them distasteful.

The alternative is intolerable. Private entities gain the power to define “hate,” “misinformation,” or “harm” according to their shifting political priorities, staff ideologies, government pressure, or advertiser demands. Tomorrow it is gender-critical feminists, critics of mass immigration, or opponents of the regulatory state. The mechanism is the same.

The Common Carrier Tradition

The common carrier doctrine provides the doctrinal bridge between free speech principles and concrete legal obligation. For centuries, Anglo-American law has recognized that certain businesses—transportation networks, telegraph lines, telephone companies, inns, and ferries—occupy such a central role in public life that they cannot refuse service to lawful customers based on the content of their message or identity. A telephone company cannot disconnect a customer because it dislikes the customer’s political calls. A railroad cannot refuse to carry freight because it disapproves of the shipper’s views. The obligation exists precisely because these entities function as chokepoints in society.

Modern social media platforms fit this definition with striking precision. They exhibit natural monopoly characteristics through network effects: the value of the platform increases with the number of users, creating winner-take-most markets that are extraordinarily difficult to displace. They have become indispensable conduits for public communication, political organizing, journalism, and economic activity. When Apple, Google, and Amazon simultaneously removed Parler from their app stores and hosting services in 2021, they demonstrated that a handful of private actors could functionally erase an entire platform and its millions of users from the internet overnight. What it cannot do is engage in viewpoint discrimination against lawful but controversial speech. This distinction is not novel; it mirrors the historical treatment of telegraph companies, which were required to transmit all lawful messages without regard to the sender’s politics.

Property Rights, Private Action, and Realism

The standard objection—that platforms are private property and therefore have absolute rights of exclusion—proves too much and ignores reality. Property rights are not absolute in any society that recognizes common carriage, public accommodations laws, or public forum doctrine. We long ago decided that a hotel cannot refuse Black customers, a restaurant cannot exclude Jews, and a telephone company cannot hang up on socialists. These restrictions on property rights were justified precisely because the businesses had taken on public character through scale and importance. The same logic applies here.

Moreover, these platforms enjoy substantial government-conferred benefits: Section 230 immunity, favorable regulatory treatment, access to government contracts, and the protection of the rule of law itself. They operate within a framework created and sustained by the public. Having accepted these benefits and achieved dominance partly through regulatory moats and network effects, they cannot claim the full immunity of a purely private social club. The right to exclude is not unlimited once an entity becomes the primary means by which citizens exercise their speech rights.

Critics warn that forced hosting will lead to worse content or drive users away. This gets the causality backwards. The current regime of selective censorship has already driven millions into more extreme, encrypted, or balkanized spaces where moderation is either absent or radically one-sided. The alternative—corporate commissars deciding what three billion people may discuss—is incompatible with liberal democracy.

The Path Forward

Legislatures should enact clear statutes designating dominant online platforms (defined by objective metrics of scale and centrality) as common carriers for lawful speech. Platforms would retain robust moderation tools against illegal content and technical abuse but would lose the power to discriminate on viewpoint. Enforcement could include expedited judicial review, significant fines calibrated to revenue, and private rights of action for users whose lawful content is suppressed. Courts should recognize that when platforms act as the functional equivalent of public forums or infrastructure, traditional First Amendment principles apply with full force.

The inclusion of hate groups in this obligation is not a bug; it is the feature that proves the principle. A free speech regime that protects only popular speech is no regime at all. The test of our commitment comes precisely when the speech is vile. Social media platforms exercise unprecedented power over human discourse. That power must be constrained by law in the same way we constrain every other form of concentrated power in a free society. Absolute free speech principles and common carrier obligations point to the same conclusion: if the speech is legal, the platforms must host it. Anything less is censorship by another name.

The public square must remain open—even to those we despise.

I. Absolute Free‑Speech as a Constitutional Baseline

1.1 The Principle of Unqualified Expression

Absolute free‑speech theory holds that any expression that is lawful — i.e., not obscene, not inciting imminent lawless action, and not defaming a specific individual with false statements — must be protected from governmental or private suppression. This view draws on the Enlightenment insight that the marketplace of ideas is self‑correcting only when all participants, however distasteful, are permitted to speak. The Supreme Court’s articulation of “the First Amendment’s command that Congress shall make no law abridging the freedom of speech” (U.S. Const. amend. 1.2 The Moral Imperative of Neutrality

If the state were to pick and choose which speech it permits, it would inevitably embed its own values into the public sphere, undermining the very notion of a neutral arena for debate. Absolute free speech, therefore, is not a permissive license for hate but a procedural safeguard: the government may not act as a censor, even when the content is morally repugnant. The moral weight of this principle lies in its insistence that truth emerges only when competing perspectives are allowed to contest one another, and that the state’s role is to protect the forum, not to police the content.

II. Common‑Carrier Obligations: Historical and Legal Foundations

2.1 The Common‑Carrier Analogy

Historically, common carriers — such as railroads, telephone companies, and later airlines — have been defined by two crucial attributes: (1) they provide a public service that is essential to societal functioning, and (2) they must treat all users equally, without discrimination based on the nature of the content they carry. The Supreme Court’s decision in Shreveport v. Louisiana (1915) affirmed that a state may not impose undue burdens on a common carrier’s ability to transmit lawful goods, reinforcing the idea that the carrier’s neutrality is a legal imperative, not a discretionary choice.

2.2 Modern Digital Platforms as De‑Facto Common Carriers

Modern social media platforms fulfill a comparable societal function: they enable the rapid, global exchange of information, organize civic participation, and serve as primary venues for news dissemination. Their scale, technical infrastructure, and network effects render them indispensable to contemporary communication. Consequently, the common‑carrier framework — requiring nondiscriminatory, universal access to the transmission service — offers a coherent legal template for regulating online services.

2.3 Statutory Precedents

Several jurisdictions have already extended common‑carrier concepts to digital platforms. The European Union’s Digital Services Act (DSA) imposes “excessively broad” obligations on “very large online platforms” to avoid arbitrary removal of lawful content, while the United States’ Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act provides immunity only when platforms act in good faith, implying a duty to retain all lawful user‑generated content absent a valid legal claim. 3.1 Safeguarding Democratic Discourse

A blanket hosting requirement would prevent the arbitrary silencing of minority or unpopular viewpoints, thereby preserving the marketplace of ideas. By obligating platforms to retain all lawful speech, the law ensures that controversial or offensive ideas can be examined, rebutted, and, ultimately, rejected through public debate rather than through pre‑emptive deplatforming. This procedural safeguard is essential for a vibrant democracy, as history demonstrates that suppression often fuels radicalization rather than attenuating it.

3.2 Maintaining Platform Neutrality

When platforms are required to host any lawful content, they are compelled to adopt a neutral, content‑agnostic stance. This reduces the incentive to employ subjective “community standards” that can be weaponized to target specific political or social groups. Neutrality, in turn, curtails the risk of covert censorship and the creation of de‑facto speech hierarchies that threaten the egalitarian nature of the public square.

This shifts the burden from continuous surveillance to targeted, judicially supervised action, a model already employed in defamation and intellectual‑property injunctions.

The convergence of absolute free‑speech doctrine and the common‑carrier tradition provides a compelling legal and philosophical foundation for requiring social media platforms and online services to host all lawful content, including speech from hate groups. The Digital Public Square: Why Social Media Platforms Must Be Legally Obligated to Host All Legal Content

An Argument for Absolute Free Speech and Common Carrier Obligations in the Digital Age

Introduction

The rise of social media platforms and online services as the dominant venues for public discourse represents the most significant transformation in the history of speech since the invention of the printing press. Platforms like Facebook, X (formerly Twitter), YouTube, and Reddit have become the modern equivalent of town squares, newspapers, and public auditoriums—spaces where ideas compete, communities form, and democratic deliberation takes place. Yet unlike the government actors constrained by the First Amendment, these private companies have assumed virtually unchecked editorial discretion over what billions of people can say and see. This essay argues that social media platforms and online services should be legally required to host all legal content—including speech from hate groups—on the basis of two interlocking principles: the philosophical imperative of absolute free speech as a precondition for a free society, and the common carrier obligations that should attach to entities functioning as critical communications infrastructure.

I. The Philosophical Foundation: Why Free Speech Must Be Absolute

The case for absolute free speech does not begin with the First Amendment; it begins with the profound insight that human beings are fallible, and that no individual, no institution, and no government possesses the infallibility required to determine which ideas should be permitted and which should be suppressed. This principle, articulated most forcefully by John Stuart Mill in On Liberty (1859), holds that silencing any opinion—no matter how odious—deprives society of the opportunity to test its own beliefs against challenge and error.

Mill argued that even if an opinion is false, its suppression robs humanity of the "clearer perception and livelier impression of truth, produced by its collision with error." What Mill understood, and what contemporary advocates of content moderation too often forget, is that the mechanism for defeating dangerous ideas is not censorship but counter-speech. The proper response to hate speech is not silence but louder, better, more persuasive speech. When society suppresses odious views, it does not eliminate them; it merely drives them underground, where they fester without scrutiny, grow unchallenged, and ultimately become far more dangerous.

The inclusion of hate groups in this framework is essential precisely because it is with the speech we most despise that the principle of free expression is most rigorously tested. The American Civil Liberties Union has long maintained that "the constitutional right to free speech is not about protecting speech that is popular or agreeable, but speech that is repugnant to many." To defend free speech only for ideas one finds palatable is not to defend free speech at all—it is to defend conformity. The commitment to free expression is truly tested not when a professor delivers an uncontroversial lecture on physics, but when a neo-Nazi seeks to march through Skokie, Illinois, or when a white supremacist group seeks to publish its views on a major platform. In those moments, society reveals whether it genuinely believes in the principle or only in its convenient application.

Critics of this position argue that speech from hate groups causes genuine harm—that it traumatizes targeted communities, incites violence, and creates hostile environments that effectively silence the very people the First Amendment was designed to protect. This concern is legitimate and should not be dismissed. But the answer to speech that silences is more speech that empowers, not the enforcement of silence by private corporations. The long, agonizing, but ultimately triumphant arc of the civil rights movement in the United States was achieved not through the suppression of racist speech but through the relentless, courageous counter-speech of those who faced hatred with moral clarity and legal argumentation. If platforms had been empowered to silence segregationists in the 1950s, they would almost certainly have also silenced civil rights activists—because the power to censor is never wielded with perfect precision or perfect justice.

II. The Common Carrier Doctrine: From Telegraphs to TikTok

The philosophical argument for absolute free speech gains crucial legal traction through the doctrine of common carriage. Common carriers are entities that serve the general public by providing essential services and, in exchange for their privileged role in the infrastructure of communication and commerce, accept obligations of non-discrimination. A telephone company cannot refuse to connect your call because it dislikes your political views. A railroad cannot refuse to carry a passenger because of their religion. A shipping company cannot decline to transport a package because of the contents of the message written inside.

The historical logic is straightforward: when a private entity becomes so deeply embedded in the infrastructure of public life that meaningful participation in society depends on access to its services, that entity ceases to function merely as a private business and begins to function as a public utility. The obligations that follow from this status are not punitive—they are the reasonable conditions attached to an extraordinary privilege: the privilege of serving as a gatekeeper to the public sphere.

In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, Congress and state legislatures applied common carrier obligations to telegraph companies, railroads, telephone networks, and airlines. The Communications Act of 1934 established that "common carriers" in telecommunications could not discriminate among users. These regulations were not seen as violations of the companies' rights—they were recognized as necessary adjustments to the reality that these companies had become indispensable to public life.

The question for the twenty-first century is obvious and unavoidable: why should the doctrine stop at the digital threshold?

Social media platforms and major online services are, for all practical purposes, the modern equivalent of the telephone network or the public square. In 2024, an estimated 5.04 billion people worldwide use social media. For many of them—particularly politicians, journalists, small business owners, activists, and marginalized communities—participation on these platforms is not a luxury but a necessity. To be excluded from Facebook, YouTube, X, or Google Search is, for a growing segment of human activity, to be excluded from public life itself. These platforms have achieved a level of market dominance and infrastructural integration that is comparable to, and in many cases exceeds, the telecommunications monopolies of the twentieth century.

Yet unlike those telecommunications monopolies, social media companies are not classified as common carriers. Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act (1996) immunizes platforms from liability for user-generated content while simultaneously allowing them to moderate content in "good faith." This statutory framework was a reasonable accommodation for the early internet—a time when platforms were small, experimental, and genuinely serving as neutral conduits. But the internet of 2024 bears no resemblance to the internet of 1996. The platforms have grown into the most powerful communication infrastructure in human history, and the legal framework governing them has not evolved to match the reality it is supposed to regulate.

The solution is not to repeal Section 230—as some have proposed, which would only suppress speech by creating excessive liability for platforms. Rather, the solution is to extend common carrier obligations to platforms with dominant market positions, requiring them to host all legal content without discrimination. This is not a radical proposal; it is a logical extension of centuries of legal reasoning about the obligations that attend public infrastructure.

III. The Problem with Content Moderation

Every argument in favor of platform-moderated speech must confront an uncomfortable and perhaps irresolvable problem: who watches the watchmen?

When a private corporation decides what speech is permissible on a platform used by billions of people, it exercises a form of power that is unprecedented in human history. The decisions of a few hundred content moderators in Dublin, San Francisco, or Hyderabad determine whether a political dissident in Myanmar can reach the world, whether a journalist in Turkey can publish the truth, and whether a scientist challenging orthodoxy can share her research. These decisions are made according to terms of service agreements that are vague, inconsistently enforced, and frequently shaped by political, commercial, and cultural pressures that have nothing to do with the principles of free expression.

The evidence of the arbitrariness and unreliability of platform moderation is overwhelming. Studies have documented systematic biases in content enforcement, with speech from certain political perspectives being disproportionately flagged, removed, or throttled. Whistleblower accounts from former employees of major platforms have revealed that moderation decisions are frequently driven by public relations concerns and advertiser preferences rather than principled commitments to safety or accuracy. During elections, during pandemics, and during social upheaval, platforms have repeatedly demonstrated that their moderation choices reflect corporate timidity rather than responsible stewardship.

Moreover, the very concept of "responsible moderation" is built on a false premise: that there exists a neutral, technically competent standard for distinguishing "harmful" speech from "acceptable" speech. In reality, speech is contextual, culturally situated, and deeply contested. What is hateful in one jurisdiction is protected in another. What is misinformation to one authority is truth to another. The attempt to impose a universal standard of acceptable speech on a global, multicultural, multilingual platform is not merely difficult—it is conceptually incoherent. The inevitable result is not neutral moderation but the arbitrary exercise of private power over public speech.

Those who advocate for platform moderation as an alternative to common carrier obligations are, whether they recognize it or not, advocating for a system in which unaccountable corporate executives exercise quasi-governmental censorship powers without any of the due process protections, transparency requirements, or democratic accountability that constrain actual governments. This is not a system that free people should accept.

IV. The State Action Doctrine and the Privatization of Censorship

A particularly troubling dimension of the current landscape is the phenomenon scholars have termed the "state action" or "governmentalization" of platform censorship. In recent years, a substantial body of evidence has emerged revealing that government officials, including senior figures in the United States executive branch, have directly pressured social media platforms to remove, suppress, and deplatform specific speakers and viewpoints. The revelations from the so-called "Twitter Files," court filings in Murthy v. Missouri (2023), and congressional testimony have documented a systematic campaign in which federal agencies flagged content for removal and applied coercive pressure—sometimes threatening antitrust enforcement, regulatory action, or revocation of Section 230 protections—to achieve compliance.

This practice raises profound constitutional concerns. When the government pressures a private entity to suppress speech it could not constitutionally suppress directly, the private entity's actions become attributable to the state for purposes of the First Amendment. The Supreme Court has repeatedly held that the government cannot use "coercion, threats, or the promise of benefits" to achieve through private actors what the Constitution forbids it from doing directly. And yet, through the mechanism of platform moderation, governments have found precisely this backdoor—a way to achieve broad censorship of constitutionally protected speech while maintaining plausible deniability.

If platforms were classified as common carriers required to host all legal content, this backdoor would be closed. Government officials could not pressure platforms to suppress speech because platforms would have no discretion to suppress. The result would be a restoration of the constitutional order: government speech restrictions would have to be imposed transparently, publicly, and subject to judicial review—rather than through opaque pressure on private intermediaries.

V. Addressing Counterarguments

Opponents of the common carrier model raise several objections, each of which deserves serious engagement and each of which, upon examination, proves insufficient.

"Platforms are private companies with First Amendment rights to editorial discretion." This is perhaps the most common objection, but it is ultimately a non-sequitur. While platforms do retain some degree of First Amendment protection—specifically, the right to exercise editorial judgment in the curation of their own speech—this right does not extend to the suppression of third-party speech on a platform that functions as a public forum. The Supreme Court has long recognized that the right of editorial discretion is constrained when the entity in question serves as an indispensable conduit for public expression. Newspapers have editorial discretion because they write the articles; telephone companies do not because they merely connect speakers. Platforms that function as digital town squares are closer to telephone companies than to newspapers.

"Requiring platforms to host hate speech will lead to real-world violence." The empirical evidence does not support this claim. Platforms that have hosted virtually unrestricted speech—including 4chan and 8kun—have not produced measurably more violence than platforms with aggressive moderation policies. Conversely, history's most catastrophic acts of violence have occurred in societies with extensive censorship apparatuses. The relationship between speech and violence is far more complex than the simple equation "speech leads to violence" suggests. What is clear is that laws against direct, specific, and imminent incitement to violence (the Brandenburg v. Ohio standard) already prohibit the most dangerous forms of speech. The speech that censoring advocates most frequently target—general bigotry, offensive opinions, extremist ideology—these are precisely the forms of expression that the First Amendment was designed to protect.

"Users are free to use alternative platforms if they object to a particular company's moderation policies." This argument ignores the reality of network effects and market concentration. If a small fraction of the internet's infrastructure were controlled by, say, five electric companies, and all five refused to serve the same category of customer, that customer would have no meaningful alternative. The same logic applies to social media. The dominance of major platforms means that deplatforming is functionally equivalent to exile from the public sphere, regardless of the theoretical availability of alternative platforms.

VI. Conclusion: The Imperative of Digital Infrastructure

We stand at a peculiar moment in the history of free expression. For the first time in human history, the dominant venues for public discourse are privately owned, commercially operated, and largely unaccountable to the public. The extraordinary concentration of communicative power in the hands of a small number of corporations represents a challenge to free speech that the Framers of the Constitution could not have anticipated—but that the legal tradition of common carriage, refined over centuries, is well-equipped to address.

The principle is simple and powerful: when a private entity becomes the infrastructure of public discourse, it must serve the public interest in discourse. This does not mean that platforms cannot set reasonable, content-neutral standards—prohibiting spam, malware, and illegal content such as CSAM and genuine incitements to imminent violence. It means that platforms cannot serve as arbiters of acceptable opinion, deciding which political views, which cultural perspectives, and which ideological commitments are worthy of public expression.

To argue otherwise—to argue that a handful of Silicon Valley executives should have the power to determine which legal ideas billions of people can access—is to argue for a form of censorship that is unprecedented in its scope, unaccountable in its operation, and antithetical to everything free societies claim to value. The common carrier model does not represent a limitation on free speech; it represents a restoration of it—a recognition that the right to speak freely is hollow when the infrastructure of speech is privately owned and privately controlled.

The digital public square belongs to the public. It is time the law reflected that reality.

The Slippery Slope Is Real

Let me be clear about what I am not saying. I am not saying that hateful ideas are without consequence. They are dangerous. They are corrosive. History has taught us that with devastating clarity.

But I am asking you to consider a harder, more uncomfortable truth: the mechanism we build today to silence ideas we despise will inevitably be turned against ideas we cherish.

Today, it is white supremacist content. Tomorrow, it may be labor organizing. The day after, it may be Palestinian solidarity, or pro-choice advocacy, or climate activism. The categories shift with every election cycle, with every moral panic, with every CEO's personal politics.

The ACLU once defended the right of Nazis to march in Skokie. Not because they endorsed Nazism — but because they understood that rights only exist when they protect the most unpopular speech. A right that applies only to popular ideas is no right at all.

We regulate utilities. We regulate broadcasters. We regulate financial institutions — not because the government knows best, but because concentrated private power over public life must answer to the public.
